"While still in Jakobsdorf he began his distance studies in mathematics and physics. After completing his studies he worked in Bucharest at the 'Research Institute for the Electrotechnical Industry'. As a pensioner he then returned to Schönberg to spend the evening of his life here, where he unfortunately died far too early." His brother Dr Hans Reiner (lawyer) 1 Sep 1946: 67. Rector Reiner is not satisfied with the prebend (allowance in kind). He also demands breakfast and supper. It is resolved that he be paid 1 litre of milk daily from the church funds. Called into the meeting, Reiner is not satisfied with this. He is given time to think it over until 3 September. Churchwarden Widmann points out that the community could lose the teacher. "The agitation grows so great that Klockner reminds them that the presbytery is deliberating in the house of God, and asks that more regard be paid to the sanctity of this place." The resolution is overturned and it is resolved to give Reiner only ½ litre of milk, but supper in the households. Called into the meeting again, teacher Reiner declares himself in agreement. From the memoirs of Martin Reiner: After his release from prison Martin Reiner wrote down his memoirs. In them he also deals with the events of 1953. He further describes the intrigues that led to his arrest and conviction, life as a political prisoner, and the difficult reintegration into life after his release. He reports in the third person and calls himself Martin. Some extracts relevant to the subject from the manuscript left by Reiner are reproduced below. 1952 - Martin took over all the mathematics and physics teaching. The school was organised as a school centre for several surrounding communities, Magarei, Probstdorf, Roseln, Hundertbücheln, Neithausen and Neustadt, and therefore also had a boarding house. Martin took his meals there. Because after about three weeks the question of his accommodation had still not been resolved, he furnished a small room in the former castle-keeper's dwelling at his own expense and moved in. At first this was meant only as a temporary makeshift, but Martin soon had to realise that he could expect nothing from the People's Council. Since it was a detached, and therefore cold, little room, he had the village carpenter fit a double window. At the beginning of this school year Martin enrolled in the three-year course in the Russian language, which was held within the framework of the school centre. He needed this knowledge of the language because Russian had been introduced as a compulsory subject at the university. He completed the first year of the course with an examination in June 1953 with the grade "Very good". Otherwise this whole period was filled with intensive study of his required reading for the second university year. He spent almost his entire salary on buying books and on consultations in higher mathematics in Kronstadt, where he often travelled. He could afford this because he had his sisters Anna and Elisabeth there, where he received board and lodging free of charge, as they maintained cordial family relations with one another. Through visiting the house of his brother-in-law Erich Tartler, where Ioan Samoila and Ioan Golea were also living incognito, he got to know them. He had first learned of their existence from his brother Wilhelm in the spring of 1952. The two had threatened Wilhelm with death by shooting because he had passed on knowledge of their presence to Martin, which had caused Wilhelm to flee hastily to Schönberg. On the way he had also looked Martin up in Großschenk but said nothing to him; yet Martin had noticed from the haste with which Wilhelm wanted to go on to Schönberg on foot, although a bus was going there in an hour, that something was wrong. 1953 - When Martin stayed with Elisabeth in Kronstadt in May 1953 for the last time before the examinations, and from there also paid Anna a visit, there was great anxiety. Ioan Samoila, alias Ioan Anghel, who had been living with brother-in-law Erich Tartler for some time and whom Martin had also got to know there, had been looked for there by the militia (police) a few days before. Brother-in-law Erich, who knew from Martin that he was travelling back to Schönberg, deeply worried and with forebodings of evil, asked him to break his journey in Voila, travel to Viktoriastadt and tell the brother of Ioan Samoila, who was a foreman at the chemical works, to come to Kronstadt immediately to solve the urgent problem of rehousing Samoila. In view of this difficult situation Martin could do nothing else but travel to Viktoriastadt and then continue his journey to Schönberg. On 1 Jul 1953 the "university examination season - month of July" began in Klausenburg. Martin went there and passed all the examinations of the second year of study successfully. Afterwards, in order to recover, do some shopping and attend cultural events, he went to Kronstadt for ten days. Since his two nieces Gerlinde Buchholzer and Helga Reiner from Temeschburg were staying with Anna at the same time for a change of air, Martin stayed with Elisabeth. His brother Wilhelm, who had meanwhile settled in Heldsdorf and worked as a driver for a transport company in Kronstadt, came during a break in his driving with the bus he drove to the flat of his sister Elisabeth. Both decided to drive in this bus to their sister Anna and brother-in-law Erich to pay them a visit. As they turned into the next street, shortly beyond Elisabeth's flat, a service car of the Security Service came towards them and turned into the street in which Elisabeth lived. Martin, who attached no great importance to this circumstance, noticed that his brother Wilhelm became quite uneasy. He evidently sensed that danger was looming. They nevertheless continued their journey and stopped in front of the house of brother-in-law Erich at Wollgasse No. 8. When nobody answered the electric bell, Martin took a stone and knocked vigorously on the yard gate. At last, after quite some time, an unknown young man opened. Martin noticed at once that opposite him, about 5 m away, stood a second young man who in a strange way kept his hand in his pocket despite the great midsummer heat. The first of the men immediately shut the yard gate behind the two, quickly frisked Martin and told him not to move from the spot. Then he ordered Wilhelm to drive the bus into the yard. Brother Wilhelm, who had learned a great deal about such things in his seven years as a Russian prisoner of war, refused to drive into the yard until both were informed that they were under arrest and had to follow all instructions. Martin was led by the first of the men into the flat of brother-in-law Erich. Here there was another man in plain clothes, who at once took all Martin's identity papers from him. Meanwhile Wilhelm was also brought in by the second security officer. His papers were taken from him too. The officer informed them that sister Anna and brother-in-law Erich had been arrested and told both of them to get back into the bus and follow their service car, which brought them to the headquarters of the Security Service in Kronstadt. Here they had to wait about half an hour until Wilhelm was subjected to a short interrogation, after which their identity papers were returned to them and they were told that they were free. Martin and Wilhelm were aware that with this month of August 1953 hard times had dawned for the whole family. Martin went alone to the flat of his sister Elisabeth and lay down. For two days he ate almost nothing, was incapable of doing anything and lay in bed most of the time with his eyes open. He thought over the situation countless times and found no way out. On the third day he decided first to travel to Schönberg to break the news gently to his parents. He told his mother at once, his father somewhat later. (...) What was to be done now? Martin realised that they were completely helpless and could do nothing but wait and see how things would develop. For the time being, however, nothing happened. Under great mental strain Martin travelled to Jakobsdorf for the start of school. Here he said nothing to anyone about the arrests and carried on with his duties as usual, but was incapable of producing good results. He enrolled in the second year of the three-year course in the Russian language held within the framework of the school centre. It did not escape him that soon afterwards references about him were being gathered from all sides. But there was also a ray of hope: he was able to convince himself that he was supported by the new and wise chairman of the People's Council (mayor - author's note) A. Topa, a friend of his father's, and consequently owed him a great deal, since within the limits of his possibilities he did everything to protect Martin. Soon came the crushing news that his brother Wilhelm had also been arrested. Martin immediately travelled to Kronstadt and engaged a well-known lawyer. With him he sounded out the situation after a few days and was dismayed when he learned that for his brother's "offence" a minimum penalty of seven years' penal servitude was provided. Only a reclassification of the charges brought against him might possibly open up hopes of a lesser sentence. Naturally Martin demanded of the lawyer that he do everything, regardless of cost, simply to avert a heavy sentence. At his sister Anna's the rooms had been sealed off by the security men. But Anna's mother-in-law Johanna Tartler was still living there in her separate flat, whose rooms had also been searched. Some of Erich's and Anna's things had been left to her. Of the two she knew only that they were imprisoned separately. With this news Martin left Kronstadt and returned to Jakobsdorf. The whole family was as if paralysed. Nobody spoke much. All silently went about their work, so as to escape the constant nightmare even for short periods. Shortly after 10 Oct 1953 an extensive report appeared in the daily newspaper Neuer Weg informing the public about the Tartler case from the point of view of the Security Service. Although what was supposed to have happened could be read there in black and white, the family did not believe that the account was truthful. In addition there were all sorts of rumours, among others that Erich had been exchanged by the American secret service for a Romanian spy, only the Security Service could not admit this to the public, hence the differently worded newspaper report. The so-called trial of the principal culprits was followed by the group trials of the accomplices and helpers, in the course of which the court hearing against Wilhelm also came up. Martin again travelled to Kronstadt. There, urged by his lawyer, he made contact with the security officer responsible for Wilhelm's case, a Captain Olteanu. The result was that, if Martin agreed to the sale of Erich's BMW motorcycle, which was registered in Martin's name, a reclassification of the charge would be attempted. Martin did not hesitate for a moment, for thus there was a prospect for Wilhelm of getting off with a minimum sentence of two years. The trial of his sister Anna had for the time being been adjourned. The family did not even know where Anna was being held in custody. Soon afterwards Martin received a letter from Erich's mother asking him to visit her. Again Martin travelled to Kronstadt. This time the final court hearing against Wilhelm had been scheduled. He was sentenced to two years' penal servitude with confiscation of his property. After the sentence was pronounced Martin went to Erich's mother. She still did not believe that her son Erich had been shot, and claimed to know from a reliable source that he was alive. At the moment, since nothing of Erich's and Anna's property had yet been taken away, she was busy passing off as much of it as possible as her own property or simply removing it. A guard had been posted in the farmyard by the People's Council (mayor's office - author's note); all buildings were locked and sealed. She knew, however, of a secret entrance into the workshop and had meanwhile also found out that the guard went every day at exactly 12 o'clock to eat at the state farm opposite and stayed there for at least an hour. With her support Martin now began to take many valuable machine parts and apparatus out of the workshop. Among them was also a dismantled, complete 750 cc BMW motorcycle. At first everything was stored in the rooms in such a way that the guard noticed nothing of the changes. Then Martin made contact with Franz Szasz, the Hungarian boy who had been brought up by Martin's parents. With him, so as not to be seen, late in the evening in the dark, he smuggled the salvaged inventory and the motorcycle with a handcart into the attic of Elisabeth's flat. Likewise, assuming that his sister Anna would soon be released, he brought part of her personal inventory to Elisabeth's. Afterwards he discussed the matter with his lawyer and agreed with him, since they assumed that Anna would not likewise be sentenced to confiscation of her property, to get her confiscated inventory released from the authorities by means of a separate court procedure. Once again this meant that Martin had to travel to Kronstadt three times for this purpose, and on the last journey also pay for two witnesses from Schönberg (Katharina Salmen and Anna Salmen-Lurz). He spent his entire income, together with all the contributions from his mother, on this. Their principle was to commit everything to save what could be saved. (...) On 1 Jul 1954 the summer examination season began at the university in Klausenburg. Martin went there and passed all the examinations of the 3rd year of study successfully. With this his course of study was completed except for the state examination. On 15 Sep 1954 the new school year 1954/1955 began. It was at the same time also his fourth university year, for which he had enrolled at the University of Bucharest. Very complicated theoretical mathematical-physical questions had to be solved. Martin realised that he could not manage this alone in remote Jakobsdorf. This first decided him to take the state examination at the pedagogical faculty of mathematics and physics in Klausenburg, so as to have a qualification in hand, and only then to devote all his attention to the next year of study. (...) In order finally to become free of the scourge of his "social origin", which constantly stood in the way of any advancement, Martin succeeded in obtaining from the People's Council (town hall - author's note) of the community of Jakobsdorf a certificate showing that he belonged to the social category "worker in the teaching profession". In order to make sure that the People's Council of his home community of Schönberg also concurred with this view, he applied there too for a confirmation worded in this way. Here, however, his adversary Anton Prescurea was chairman (mayor - author's note), and he was by no means inclined to grant Martin this "favour". He promptly handed him a certificate stating that Martin's parents had formerly "been kulaks, but at present belong to the [working] class". This showed that such categorisations (classifications - author's note) were arbitrarily left to individual persons who acted as they pleased, and woe betide anyone if they were ill-disposed towards him. (...)
On 1 Jul 1955 the state examination of the pedagogical section of the faculty of mathematics and physics began in Klausenburg. Martin passed it successfully and, immediately after the last examination, travelled to Bucharest in order to take some further examinations at the faculty of mathematics and physics there as well. (...) On 15 Sep 1955 the pupils of the surrounding communities gathered once again at the Jakobsdorf school centre. As a graduate of the pedagogical faculty of mathematics and physics, Martin was now the best-qualified teacher in the school. The pupils were grateful to him for his work. He devoted himself entirely to his profession, without, however, losing sight of the question of his further education. In Bucharest, during his examination season, he had made contact with Mathias Müller, the chief censor of the German-language press. On his advice to apply for a post in Bucharest, Martin wanted first to complete his studies. For this purpose he applied for four months' unpaid leave in order to attend lectures in mathematics and physics at the University of Bucharest. The leave was granted, and so Martin went to Bucharest, where he lived with an acquaintance. After passing the university examinations he also visited, among other places, the German school in Bucharest. Headmaster Jakob Neumann asked him to apply for the vacant post of mathematics and physics teacher. Martin wrote the appropriate application and travelled back to Schönberg convinced that his application would not be approved by the school authority of the capital. On 15 Sep 1956 the new school year began. In order to await the decision, Martin applied to the competent school authority in Agnetheln for his release, on the grounds that he wished to be transferred to Bucharest. The authority granted his request but, since it did not believe Martin would succeed, kept his teaching post in Jakobsdorf open for him. Martin went to Bucharest, and in only three days all the necessary documents for his transfer and removal to Bucharest were issued to him. The Agnetheln school authority and his colleagues in Jakobsdorf were speechless. (...) In Jakobsdorf Martin left behind a circle of good friends, men and women. He had got on best with his colleagues Josef Polder, Kuno Martini, Helga Wolf and Anna Wagner. He also owed a great deal to his friends from the Kränzchen (social circle) Katharina Balthes, Emma Duldner and Mathilde Schuller. The school year 1956/1957 was marked by strenuous work. On the one hand Martin was now teaching at a secondary school for the first time, which required thorough preparation for the lessons. On the other hand he had to get used to big-city life. He succeeded in mastering everything. For extracurricular activity he was recommended by the school authority to the Society for Mathematical and Physical Sciences in the Romanian People's Republic, to be admitted as a member. Likewise he was called upon by the Institute for Pedagogical Sciences to work within the pedagogical lectureships. In addition he was officially to take part in the district conferences of the Committee for the Struggle for Peace. He also volunteered as an activist of the Bucharest cultural centre "Friedrich Schiller". (...) In April 1957, at the instigation of his former Hermannstadt classmate Fritz Wächter, Martin moved to the courtyard where the latter also lived. Here Martin found contact with German families and felt secure. Outside school he maintained close relations with the family of Fritz Wächter and with their friends Gertrud Sill, Hedwig Capesius, Julia Markovitsch, Ingrid Markus, Sonja Mateescu and Hariclia Titu. (...) He completed the fifth year of university study and, together with his fellow student Hans Lang from Heltau, prepared for the final examination, which he passed successfully in July 1958, thereby acquiring the title of Diplom-Physiker (graduate physicist). (...) At the start of the new school year 1958/1959 the German school was moved from Strada Luterană No. 2 to Nuferilor Street No. 56, since the old site was being demolished in order to begin the large reconstruction works around the Palace of the Republic. (...) Headmaster Jakob Neumann was transferred to the Ministry of Education as a school inspector. Johanna Henning ran the school provisionally. The district school authority, however, intended to entrust the management of the school to a young male teacher. Martin was considered for this. For this purpose he was ordered to the inspectorate. Martin realised that it was now a matter of make or break. If he had refused immediately, that would have been disadvantageous in the circumstances. If he accepted, references would probably be gathered from all sides, and it needed only one of them to state that he had served in the Waffen-SS, and the misfortune would be complete. Martin left the decision to fate and answered the school inspector to whom he had been summoned that, should he be entrusted with the management of the gymnasium, he would "do his duty". At first things seemed to develop positively. One day, however, a Jewish colleague told him that a rumour was going round according to which Martin had served in the Waffen-SS. With that it was clear that the attempt to conceal his past had failed. He reckoned with the very worst. As it was to turn out later, Anton Prescuria was again behind the story. Time crept slowly by; Martin adopted a wait-and-see position. He was assigned to the most unpleasant tasks. First he had to go with the pupils on agricultural labour, then take part in a school outing as supervisor, and so on. On his return from the outing an invitation awaited him to report within 24 hours to the school authority of the capital. The short deadline alone boded no good. Martin presented himself; he was reproached for not having truthfully stated all the facts in his curriculum vitae and was required to supplement it then and there. What shocked Martin particularly was the obtuse question of how many Jews he had shot. After much to-ing and fro-ing, at the beginning of the school year 1959/1960 he found himself first transferred from the German school to a Romanian school. Martin accepted this, but not without first complaining to every possible office. At the same time, however, he realised that a large-scale investigation had been launched against him but had not yet been concluded. He believed that he had been transferred to the Romanian school only in order to isolate him completely from the German-speaking population of Bucharest, so that his already decided arrest would give as little cause for talk as possible within this population group, which numbered an estimated 6000 souls. The German school in Bucharest at that time had after all around 800 pupils, every one of whom had come to know and value Martin during his three years of work there. On 15 Jun 1960 the school year ended. Martin had also earned respect among his new Romanian fellow teachers. A member of the staff, a native of Constanța, had offered him free lodging for a summer holiday on the Black Sea. Martin accepted the friendly gesture and went there. On 29 Jul 1960 he returned to Bucharest, intending afterwards to make a visit to Schönberg. In his flat he found a summons to the militia to have his identity card checked. Martin noticed that he was being shadowed, i.e. watched at every step by dubious figures. He bought his ticket for the journey home, packed his suitcase and went to bed. On 1 Aug 1960, shortly after midnight, he was woken by a noise. When he opened his eyes he saw a man climbing through the open window into his room. Martin jumped out of bed and seized a chair, but the man was already holding out his identity card and introduced himself: "Captain in the Security Service"; he then pulled down the window shutters, switched on the light and opened the door. Immediately two more men entered the room. The flat was searched. Then the captain told Martin to get dressed; he had to come along, some things needed to be cleared up. When Martin was dressed, the captain said he should also take warmer clothes with him in a suitcase. Then the penny finally dropped for Martin: if a man is asked in August to take warm clothes with him in a suitcase, there can hardly be any question of a simple "clarification" ahead. Blindfolded, Martin was taken in a car that was waiting at the corner to the Ministry of the Interior and from there to the Security Service's remand prison in Uranus Street in Bucharest. On 11 Aug 1960 a house search was carried out at home in Schönberg by an investigating officer, Captain Ion Teodoru, in which some books were confiscated. (...) At a time when the violation of the most elementary procedural guarantees was method, when "evidence" was extorted by the use of physical coercion that could not be resisted, Martin had to learn all the meanings contained in the word "subhumanity". A tormenting restriction of food combined with a daily 18-hour prohibition on leaning back while sitting will ruin even the strongest person in a short time. Everything was only a question of time. After four months of "interrogations", in which the most varied means of moral and physical pressure were applied, including beatings to the point of unconsciousness, he was charged with the incident of 1953, namely that he had not only been guilty of failing to report, but had moreover supplied the agents with information and, when the operation to arrest the Jaques spy group was already in full swing, had in collaboration with the brother of Ioan Samoila, who lived in Viktoriastadt, actually tried to organise the rehousing of Ioan Samoila in order to withdraw him from arrest by the Security Service. On 10 Dec 1960 Martin was sentenced to twelve years' forced labour and to the confiscation of all his property (judgment No. 145 of 10 Dec 1960 - file No. 178/1960 of the territorial military court of Bucharest, Calea Plevnei No. 145). The sorely tried mother in her despair addressed a petition to the Presidium of the Grand National Assembly and asked for a pardon for her only child. The application was rejected under number 2719/1960. According to file 963/1961 of the competent bailiff, an inspection of his confiscated personal property was carried out in Martin's absence. A small remainder of articles of strictly personal use, protected by law, i.e. not subject to expropriation, was handed over for safekeeping on 31 Mar 1962 to his mother, who had been ordered to Bucharest specially for this purpose. The remaining part was valued by the bailiff Justinian Oprea according to the record of proceedings of 12 Oct 1960 and, since it was "used" property, sold off at giveaway prices. Total value according to the official valuation: 6944 lei, nevertheless a considerable sum for the conditions of 1960.
On 6 Jan 1960 [sic] Martin was committed to the dreaded death redoubt of Jilava, the prison for political prisoners south of Bucharest, and in the very first days of his imprisonment had to realise that the aim of incarceration here was physical annihilation, i.e. the elimination of supposed opponents of the regime. The physical resistance of every newly committed prisoner visibly melted away like snow in the sun. In the middle of winter, at temperatures below zero degrees Celsius, the prisoners were ordered naked to collect their clothing and had to wait outside in front of the relevant room until each one's turn came to receive his clothes. The beds in the communal cells were stacked in three tiers one above the other, and mostly three prisoners slept in two beds. Among the methods of psychological and physical annihilation must also be counted the "count", during which the prisoners, lined up in rows, sometimes had to stand to attention in the yard for hours. Whole books could be written about the ill-treatment by the guards and their brutality. The facilities for washing were so restricted that soon everything was thick with dirt. As far as food is concerned, it must be said that one never got rid of an extremely "burning" feeling of hunger. There were no heating problems in the rooms, for they were not heated at all. The inmates were therefore glad when the cells were overcrowded, since the air then sometimes warmed up a little. The prisoners who best survived the destructive rage of the apparatus of power were those who found in themselves the strength and the will to preserve an inner universe, i.e. who held on to a conviction that offered them a prospect of a better world, and did not let themselves be robbed of the only wealth they still had, human dignity. On 3 Apr 1961 Martin was transferred to the forced-labour camp of Luciu-Giurgeni, formation 0319, district (raion) Fetești, region of Bucharest, which lay on the bank of the left arm of the Danube. From there, with the help of political prisoners, the "Marsh of Brăila", the land between two arms of the Danube stretching from the little town of Vadu Oii to the Danube port of Brăila, was made cultivable by earth embankments and the strengthening of the Danube dykes, by the construction of irrigation systems and drainage canals in the marshy lowlands, and by building paths and roads. The living conditions to which the prisoners were exposed here hovered around the lowest limit. Tragic escape attempts, some of which ended fatally, bore witness to this. Bad food and unfiltered "drinking water" simply scooped out of the Danube caused constant diarrhoea among the prisoners. General dystrophy was the result. Martin, together with his former schoolmate Hans Bergel, held out at first. It went differently for the third friend, the surgeon Dr Livius Grecu, who simply collapsed unconscious while hoeing maize. Martin took him over his shoulder and carried him to the horse-drawn cart that had brought a barrel of water for the prisoners, so that he could be taken back to the penal colony. This assistance, which the doctor was told about afterwards, resulted in a particularly close friendship developing between the two, which continued even after their release. Martin owed a great deal to it. The conscientious medical attention constantly available to him through this friendship contributed decisively to his surviving the period of imprisonment mentally and physically. In order to squeeze the prisoners' labour even harder, part of the camp was moved into the heart of the area. The unhealthy climate prevailing there, the complete isolation from family, and the cruel little games of the guards, with which they took it out on the prisoners, were very hard on them. If, for example, a weed had been overlooked while hoeing maize, the prisoner concerned was forced by the guards, under blows, to pull it out with his teeth. This "reserve" of labour was used arbitrarily and without restriction, since the prisoners had been placed outside the law. Brutality was desired by the leadership. Working hours depended on the weather; here Martin heard for the first time that the "light-day" counted as working time. To supplement their wholly inadequate food, the prisoners ate raw maize, sunflower seeds and wild berries that they found while hoeing in the fields. To give an idea of all this, the assessment of one prisoner may be mentioned here, the engineer Titus Ghițescu, who had been deported to Auschwitz during the war and now said openly to the faces of high-ranking Security Service officers: "Auschwitz was a sanatorium compared with what is going on here, and it would be better to shoot people than to expose them to these tortures." The possibility of a legal review of his conviction was practically denied to Martin. Every six months the prisoners were allowed a sheet of paper to apply for a retrial. But without any connection to the outside world, without legal assistance, nothing could be achieved. No news, no books, no contact with relatives - the restrictions were scarcely bearable. Only later were they allowed to write postcards home. In four years Martin wrote 16 postcards, i.e. four a year, to his mother. (...) His brother Hans in Germany tried to come to the aid of his imprisoned siblings, but without any success. He was at least able to bring about that both Martin and his sister Anna were granted permission to settle in Germany. On 28 Jul 1964, after four years of hard forced labour that had led to total dystrophy, Martin was remitted the rest of his sentence on the basis of Decree No. 411/1964. He was set free and arrived in Bucharest without a single leu in his pocket. In order to be able to get about, he borrowed 100 lei from Sofia Niculescu (Braisch) and began to look around in Bucharest. The first great blow he felt was the loss of his flat. It had meanwhile been occupied by a woman named Paula Petalla. She proved accommodating, however, and allowed Martin to sleep in his former kitchen, which was also a walk-through room. He submitted the necessary applications for reinstatement in the teaching profession and travelled to Schönau [sic] to his mother. Arriving home, he had to realise that the period of dehumanisation to which he had been exposed had changed him. When one has to live the life of an animal for four years, one cannot return as the person one was before. The human being Martin had indeed come home, but only as an outward remnant; mental scars had been inflicted on him that remained, marks of the four years that could not be removed. In Schönberg he first began to gather together his remaining household goods, i.e. to put in order what was left of them. (...) Then Martin went back to Bucharest and left nothing untried at the school authority of the capital to obtain a post as a teacher. On 23 Sep 1964 the ban on practising his profession finally came: Martin was informed in writing that he should look for a post in another field of work. It struck him like lightning. But life had to go on, despite the loss of his livelihood. Yet further difficulties arose as a consequence of his imprisonment. Even if Martin was officially not supposed to be subject to any restrictions in public life, great difficulties were nevertheless put in the way of his reintegration into public life, thanks to the inertia of the administrative apparatus. Every petty state official believed it was positively his duty to put obstacles in the way of a former political prisoner, let alone support him or grant him concessions, all of this of course in order to "look good" in the eyes of the relevant cadre department. Even if many a state official privately had a benevolent smile to spare for Martin, he could never count on a favourable outcome of his written submissions. First of all the housing question awaited its solution, extremely oppressively. In Bucharest in those years one could only obtain accommodation through the housing office, since buying a flat was hardly possible and, for Martin, lacking any means whatsoever, was quite out of the question, for he owned literally nothing. At the housing office they had nothing but a shrug of the shoulders for him. So he set up a place to sleep in his former kitchen and devoted himself to the vitally important and oppressive question of a new career. The competent labour office did accept his application, but did nothing for months, until Martin turned directly to the Council of Ministers. After three months he was then offered three jobs, namely: at the Petroaia quarry, Dâmbovița county, 78 km from Bucharest, as a rate-setter at a salary of 1050-1350 lei; at the state trading enterprise "Bijuteria" as an assistant bookkeeper for 700-800 lei a month; and at the enterprise "Întreprinderea de Prospecțiuni Geologice și Geofizice" as a travelling worker throughout the country for a monthly income of 800 to 850 lei. Naturally none of these jobs was suitable for a person with two university degrees, so Martin declined. But then he realised that this was exactly what had been expected of him, so that they could report to the Council of Ministers that they had indeed offered him three jobs but he had accepted none of them. Finally on 10 Nov 1964 he was sent to ISCAS, the Research and Design Institute for Building, Architecture and Systematisation. Here too the job offered and the pay did not correspond to his professional training, but Martin raised no objection, since the workplace could be reached on foot in only ten minutes from his lodging and he wanted at last to find a place, so as to look around afterwards for new opportunities calmly and in good time. At ISCAS he worked in the "cost estimates" studio for apartment-block construction. With this began his difficult path of reintegration into normal life." Thus: Karl-Heinz Brenndörfer: "Banditen, Spione oder Helden? Bewaffneter antikommunistischer Widerstand in Rumänien 1948-1962" ["Bandits, Spies or Heroes? Armed Anti-Communist Resistance in Romania 1948-1962"] (pp. 258-269, with small changes by the author himself on 11 Jan 2009 compared with the book). 22 Sep 1946. 86. R193a [Hätte folgen müssen, gemäß Index: P.126 Rochus Andreas, die Seite wurde jedenfalls überblättert, sie fehlt hier. L193 beginnt mit II. „An Weingärten“ ungewöhnlich, denn sonst ist I. Status Passivus und II. Status Activus mit irgendeiner Spezifikation.] Aus dem Kopf ist ersichtlich, dass unter die Witwe, Andreas, Michael und Anna geteilt wurde. R193: „V An Vieh 60 Ein Paar Joch Ochsen 83 hiervon erhält die Tochter Anna Rfl. 25 W.W. gegen den Vorempfang der Brüder dann kommt noch zu theilen 58“ = 19,20 Witwe + 3 x 12,53 ½ „61 Eine Ziege 2,30 Vorräthige Frucht erhält jedes Kind 1 Küb. Kukurautz und ¾ Hafer. Das Korn ist ausgestreut und soll nach der Ernd getheilt werden. Die Hochzeit Unkösten versprechen die Brüder der Schwester tragen zu helfen. Der Wohnhof vic. Joh: Schuster 93 hirvon wird an Dafir [?] Rumdyrgast [?] mit Rfl 13 xr 8 dann kommt noch zu theilen 80,52“ [26,40 der Witwe und je 26,40 Michael und Anna] „Der Gatter [?] Hof vic. Mich: Gull 40“ davon 13,20 der Witwe und 26,40 an Andreas. L194 „Mit der Kirchen Kleidung sind die Kinder verglich so gar daß nach dem sich die Söhne solche von Ihren Dienst Löhnen gekauft haben, so hat sich die Tochter die Kirsen ebenfals von Ihrem verdienten diesjährigen Dienst Lohn zu kaufen. Vom Hans Roth nehmen die Söhne Ihren Anthel so gleich in besitz. Die Tochter erhält folgende Eine Sense, Eine Häjer [?], Eine Eiserne Heu Gabel, Ein Brand Eisen, Ein hintz [?] Gestell, Ein hint. Wagen Rad, Eine Leinen Guib [?], Ein alten Kirchen peltz, fier wollene Guib, 2 Frucht Küb., 2 Polster nebst überzügen, Einen Ramptisch hir von hat sieh dem Bruder Andreas 50 kr. zurück zu zahlen, fier alte Trugel, Eine altes Bank, Eine Eiserne Ladingschwach [?], Ein 14 E. Käßel, Ein fier Schäfel, Ein Eßig Fäßel von 2 Emern.“ „Anmerkung: Da Hof vic. Mich: Gull der Aussage nach noch nicht ganz in Richtigkeit sein soll, so haben Mich: und Anna fals Andreas zum zahlen hirvon gehalten werde, demselben bei zu steiern. Tutor der Ana ist die Mutter vom Theil Amt bestelt.“ Hochzeit der Anna schien aber schon geplant, s.o.

R193a [According to the index, P.126 Rochus Andreas should have followed here; in any case the page was skipped over, it is missing here. L193 begins with II. "Vineyards", which is unusual, for otherwise I. is Liabilities and II. Assets with some specification.] From the heading it can be seen that the division was among the widow, Andreas, Michael and Anna. R193: "V. Livestock: 60. A pair (yoke) of oxen 83; of this the daughter Anna receives 25 Rhenish florins Viennese currency against the advance receipt of the brothers; then there remains to be divided 58" = 19.20 widow + 3 x 12.53 ½. "61. A goat 2.30. Of the produce in stock each child receives 1 Kübel of maize and ¾ of oats. The rye is sown and is to be divided after the harvest. The brothers promise to help their sister bear the wedding expenses. The residential farmstead, neighbour (vic.) Joh[ann] Schuster, 93; of this [is paid] to Dafir [?] Rumdyrgast [?] 13 Rhenish florins 8 kreuzer; then there remains to be divided 80.52" [26.40 to the widow and 26.40 each to Michael and Anna]. "The Gatter [?] farmstead, neighbour Mich[ael] Gull, 40"; of this 13.20 to the widow and 26.40 to Andreas. L194: "With regard to church clothing the children are settled, indeed so that, since the sons bought theirs from their service wages, the daughter likewise has to buy the Kirsen [garment] from her earned service wages of this year. From Hans Roth the sons take possession of their share at once. The daughter receives the following: a scythe, a Häjer [?], an iron hay fork, a branding iron, a back [?] frame, a back wagon wheel, a linen Guib [?], an old church fur coat, four woollen Guib, 2 grain Kübel, 2 cushions with covers, a frame table (Ramptisch), of which she has to pay back 50 kreuzer to her brother Andreas, four old chests, an old bench, an iron Ladingschwach [?], a 14-Eimer cauldron, a four-Schäfel [vessel], a vinegar cask of 2 Eimer." "Note: Since the farmstead, neighbour Mich[ael] Gull, according to statements is not yet entirely in order, Mich[ael] and Anna, should Andreas be held to pay for it, are to contribute towards it. The mother has been appointed guardian of Anna by the estate-division office." Anna's wedding, however, seemed already to be planned, see above.

Amte Gesetzmäßig aufgetheilt worden wie folgt. Status Passivus Bei Popa Ion Greck eine Wiese verfpändet 40 dieser betrag wird auf das in Händen habende Pfand angewiesen.“ L221: An Vieh: Eine rote Stutte 30, roter Wallach, 55, rotbraune Stutte 35, schwarzer 4- jähriger Hengst 30, rotes 2-jähriges Fohlen 30, weiße 3-jährige Kuh, 5 Schafe 20, 2 junge Schafe 5, 2 Borstige 8, 4 Borstige 16, 6 Ferkel 12. R221: „165 Ein lederner Sattel 4 170 Der Webstuhl samt Zugehör 3“ Bettzeug „Vom Leinzeug nehmen die 2 verheiratheten Kinder ihren Antheil in besitz. Die 3 Ledigen erhalten jedes 1 Strohsack, 1 grobes Leintuch, 2 hanfene und 1 baumwollenes Manshemde, u. ein gestreiftes Tischtuch. Mit der übrigen Kleidung sind die Kinder dahin verglichen, die 3 Aeltesten haben solche empfangen, und zur Anschaffung solcher für die 2 jüngsten bleibt der Witwe und Mutter geschätzt auf Rfl. 35 W.W. Vom Erdenen Geschirr erhält jedes Kind 4 Krüge und 2 Teller.“ L222: „Von der vorräthigen Frucht erhält jedes Kind 2/4 Korn, 1 Kübel Kukurautz und 2/4 Hafer im Vertrauen [?] der Mutter bleiben nebst ihrem gebührenden 3ten Theil noch 5 Kübel zur bestllung der Hochzeiten der 3 noch unverheyratheten Kinden. Der Wohnhoff welcher vermöge letzwilliger Verordnung des Vaters nach dem derselbe sehr groß ist in 2 Theile getheilt wo von die obere helfte der jüngste Sohn Johann, die untere helfte der Sohn Martin besitzen sollen, wird folgendermaßen geschätzt. Die Obere Helfte 90 30 12 12 12 12 12 Die untere Helfte 63 21 8,24 8,24 8,24 8,24 8,24“

L218: P137 "On 26 December 1847, following the death of the local inhabitant Michael Rochus, his estate was lawfully divided by the village [...?] office among the widow and the 5 surviving children, namely the son Michael, the daughter Catharina, the daughter Anna, the son Martin aged 16 and the son Johan aged 10, as follows. Liabilities: a meadow pledged to Popa Ion Greck 40; this amount is assigned against the pledge he holds." L221: Livestock: a red mare 30, red gelding 55, red-brown mare 35, black 4-year-old stallion 30, red 2-year-old foal 30, white 3-year-old cow, 5 sheep 20, 2 young sheep 5, 2 pigs 8, 4 pigs 16, 6 piglets 12. R221: "165. A leather saddle 4. 170. The loom with accessories 3." Bedding. "Of the linen the 2 married children take possession of their share. The 3 unmarried ones each receive 1 straw mattress, 1 coarse sheet, 2 hempen and 1 cotton man's shirt, and a striped tablecloth. With the remaining clothing the children are settled thus: the 3 eldest have received theirs, and for procuring such for the 2 youngest, an amount valued at 35 Rhenish florins Viennese currency remains with the widow and mother. Of the earthenware each child receives 4 jugs and 2 plates." L222: "Of the produce in stock each child receives 2/4 rye, 1 Kübel of maize and 2/4 oats; in trust [?] of the mother there remain, besides her due third share, another 5 Kübel for arranging the weddings of the 3 still unmarried children. The residential farmstead, which by virtue of the father's last will, since it is very large, is divided into 2 parts, of which the youngest son Johann is to possess the upper half and the son Martin the lower half, is valued as follows. The upper half 90 30 12 12 12 12 12. The lower half 63 21 8.24 8.24 8.24 8.24 8.24"

Hausnummer 11: Rochus Georg, seine Frau eine geborene Schappes, ein urwüchsiger Schlag von Menschen, kräftig und robust. Seine Söhne ebenfalls. Der Älteste, wie immer, Georg, gefolgt von Michael Martin, Johann und Thomas. Dazwischen eine Tochter, die Katharina. Auf dem Hof blieb der Johann, auf die anderen komme ich noch zurück. Der Johann, seine Frau Frieda geb. Frank, ihre Kinder, der Hans ( übrigens, auf den habe ich als Junge aufgepaßt, die Kühe sollten ihn nicht treten beim Maishacken auf dem Ruidenleund), dann kam die Frieda und der Martin. Johann Rochus war Stellmacher (Wagner) von Beruf und hat so manchem Roseiner die Wagen instandgesetzt. Er war ein sehr perfekter Handwerker und ein guter Fachmann. War nach dem Kriege lange Jahre in Österreich geblieben und seine Frau hat die Kinder großgezogen, mit viel Fleiß und von ihrer Hände Arbeit. Ein angeborener Humor hat sie stets begleitet und sie war die gute Tante Frieda in der ganzen Gasse. Wenn die Kinder eine Herberge für irgendeine Feier suchten, dann gingen sie zu Tante Frieda. Ihr Ältester hat diesen Humor mitbekommen und hat sich einmal ein tolles Ding geleistet. Der Bruder der Frieda, Frank Johann, war in dem Haus versteckt, nach dem Kriege jagte die Miliz hinter den Heimkehrern her, um sie ins Bergwerk zu stecken. Johann hielt sich überwiegend im Keller auf. Eines Abends hat er dann mal mit seiner Schwester am Tisch gesessen, der kleine Hans hat die Haustür geöffnet mit den Worten :" Ja, Herr Wachtmeister, mein Onkel ist hier." Der Johann Frank ist fluchtartig durch die Luke in den Keller gerumpelt, hat sich bald alle Knochen gebrochen, kam nur wieder hoch als er hörte, daß seine Schwester den Kleinen verdrosch. Nachts schlief der Frank im Hause, konnte diese Nacht aber nicht einschlafen, der Schreck lag ihm noch in den Knochen und unter Stöhnen hat er einige Male gesagt." Frieda, schlag' den Kerl doch tot." Der Hans kam auf seine Mutter, mit Sinn für Humor, wogegen der Martin ganz der Vater ist. Es ist erfreulich, festzustellen, wenn der Sohn so ganz und gar der Vater ist. Ich habe den Martin 20 Jahre lang nicht gesehen. Auf einer Hochzeit sah ich ihn plötzlich vor mir stehen mit dem Kommentar:" Mensch, Martin, du bist aber ganz der Vater." Martin hat eine Merglerin (Leawendich) geheiratet und hat drei Mädchen. Mit den Rochus verbindet mich eine Freundschaft, wie mein Urgroßvater mit dem alten Rochus von gegenüber. Die hätten in einer Nacht einen Eimer Wein gesoffen.

House No. 11: Rochus Georg, his wife née Schappes, a natural, sturdy breed of people, strong and robust. His sons likewise. The eldest, as always, Georg, followed by Michael, Martin, Johann and Thomas. In between a daughter, Katharina. Johann stayed on the farmstead; I shall come back to the others. Johann, his wife Frieda née Frank, their children: Hans (by the way, I looked after him as a boy, so that the cows would not tread on him while we were hoeing maize on the Ruidenleund), then came Frieda and Martin. Johann Rochus was a wheelwright (Wagner) by trade and repaired the wagons of many a Roseln man. He was a very accomplished craftsman and a good expert. After the war he stayed in Austria for many years, and his wife brought up the children with great diligence and by the work of her own hands. An innate sense of humour always accompanied her, and she was the good Aunt Frieda of the whole street. When the children were looking for a place to hold some celebration, they went to Aunt Frieda. Her eldest inherited this humour and once pulled a terrific stunt. Frieda's brother, Frank Johann, was hidden in the house; after the war the militia were hunting the men returning home in order to put them in the mines. Johann stayed mostly in the cellar. One evening he was sitting at the table with his sister, when little Hans opened the front door with the words: "Yes, Sergeant, my uncle is here." Johann Frank tumbled headlong through the hatch into the cellar, nearly breaking every bone in his body, and only came up again when he heard his sister thrashing the little one. At night Frank slept in the house, but that night he could not get to sleep; the fright was still in his bones, and several times he groaned: "Frieda, just beat the fellow to death." Hans took after his mother, with a sense of humour, whereas Martin is entirely his father. It is pleasing to find a son who is so completely and utterly his father. I had not seen Martin for 20 years. At a wedding I suddenly saw him standing in front of me, with the comment: "Man, Martin, you are just like your father." Martin married a woman from Mergeln (Leawendich) and has three girls. A friendship binds me to the Rochus family, as my great-grandfather was bound to old Rochus from across the street. Those two could put away an Eimer of wine in one night.

Rochus No. 83 complains that the whole school-fee levy is being demanded of him although he is involved in divorce proceedings. - Resolution: If men and women are involved in divorce proceedings, they shall be treated like widows and widowers in the collection of school fees, levies etc. and have to pay only half of the demands." 1 Jun 1924. The details of my great-grandparents are: ROCHUS, Johann, estate manager, * Roseln (Transylvania) 15 Jan 1871, + Gattendorf (Burgenland, Austria) May 1945 (in the course of the Russian invasion, unfortunately no exact day recorded, probably 10 May). 28.12.1924. 94. 95. „Nach Eröffnung der Sitzung liest Lehrer Lautner die Berichte über die drei letzten Sitzungen des Presbyteriums vor. Nach Richtigstellung einiger kleiner Ungenauigkeiten werden sie angenommen. Nur Th. Rochus 96, den es giftet, dass in der Sitzung vom 13. Dezember über das ungebührliche Betragen seines Sohnes gesprochen wurde, protestiert gegen die Sitzung und den Bericht darüber mit der Begründung, dass er in der Sitzung nicht zugegen gewesen sei. Und das wieder begründet er damit, dass er nicht mindestens einen Tag vor der Sitzung und nicht „mit einem Programm“ eingeladen worden sei, sagt aber im selben Atem, dass er an dem Tag krank gewesen sei. Er wirft dem Pfarrer vor, dass er verfassungswidrig vorgegangen sei und ihn sekkieren wolle. - Der Pfarrer weist diese Anschuldigungen zurück und hebt hervor, dass Rochus noch immer rechtzeitig eingeladen worden sei, dass aber sein Sohn - wenn er vielleicht nur dem zuliebe doch in die Sitzung gekommen wäre - auch auf der ausführlichsten schriftlichen Einladung noch nicht habe stehen können, weil er sich eben nur unmittelbar vor der Sitzung so unverschämt benommen habe. - Rochus zankt aber weiter und wirft dem Pfarrer vor, dass er seinem Sohn den Tanz heut Abend verbieten wolle. Nun versucht Knechtvater Buchholzer 115 den Pfarrer zu bewegen, den Burschen Rochus und Röhrig die Strafe zu erlassen, wenn sie um Verzeihung bäten. - Darauf erwidert der Pfarrer, dass es keine Kunst sei, um Verzeihung zu bitten, wenn man dafür eine ganze Nacht tanzen dürfe. Immerhin sei er bereit und entschlossen gewesen, die Strafe zu schenken; wenn der letzte Zugang anders verlaufen wär, hätt er’s auch getan, aber nach diesem Zugang könne er nicht. Dann schildert er, wie nach Verkündigung der Strafe auf dem Zugang der gewesene Altknecht wie ein Bolschewik die ganze Bruderschaft habe verhetzen wollen und erklärt habe, dass dann überhaupt kein Tanz sein werde, und wie er, vom Pfarrer dafür zurechtgewiesen, noch unverschämter erwidert habe, er wolle sehn, wer ihm oder einem andern am Tanzen hindern werde. Darauf fährt aber Rochus wieder auf und ist nicht zum Schweigen zu bringen. Er mischt den Herrn Jesus in die Sache und den Herrn Bischof, der es einmal schriftlich gegeben hab, dass man einzelne Knechte vom Tanz nicht ausschließen dürfe. - Der Vorsitzer fordert ihn auf, wenn er Lust habe, auch zum Bischof zu gehen, aber jetzt endlich Ruhe zu geben. - Darauf erklärt Rochus, wenn der Pfarrer das Verbot nicht zurück ziehe, dann werde sein Sohn eben trotz des Verbotes tanzen. „Ich schicke ihn, auf meine Verantwortung tanzt der Junge heute!“ - Der Vorsitzer erwidert ihm: „Dann werden Sie aber aus dem Presbyterium hinausfliegen!“ - Nun beginnt aber Rochus erstrecht zu lamentieren: Von seinem Pflug könne ihn niemand vertreiben, er gebe seinem Jungen das Brot, und allerlei anderes unsinniges Zeug - und hört nicht mehr auf. Da schreit ihn der Vorsitzer an: „Herr Rochus, schweigen Sie jetzt!“ Aber Rochus erwidert: „Ich hab das Wort“, und will weiter zanken, hört aber doch endlich auf, als ihm der Pfarrer zuruft: „Ich hab es Ihnen genommen!“ 11.02.1925. 13. Auf Anzeige des Vorsitzers hat das BK das Disziplinarverfahren gegen Presbyter Thomas Rochus 96 angeordnet. 08.04.1925. 33. Presbyter Thomas Rochus war vor ein paar Tagen mit dem Kurator beim Pfarrer und bekannte sein unziemliches und pflichtwidriges Benehmen, bedauert es und bat um Verzeihung. Daher zog Pfarrer seine Anzeige zurück. Herr Rochus hat nur die schon aufgelaufenen Kosten zu tragen. „Noch lieber wäre es mir gewesen, wenn ich ihn gar nicht hätte anzeigen müssen, denn ich möchte in Frieden und gutem Einvernehmen mit meiner Gemeinde leben.“ 20.12.1933. Rochus 83 hat Strafe von 400 Lei, will aber nur 50 zahlen. Er hat „keinen Gehorsam gegenüber seiner Erzieher, Pfarrer und Rektor“. Er sagte „wenn ihn der Herr Rektor bestraft hätte, er auch dreingehauen hätte“. Lange unangenehme Debatte und 5 Beschlüsse: 1. Jeder Tänzer und Tänzerin nach 12 Uhr bei letztem Tanz zahlt 10 Lei. Sächsische Fahne. 2. Rochus 83 zahlt entweder 200 Lei oder darf dreimal nicht tanzen. (Je 50/Tanz. 50 erlegte er schon).

28 Dec 1924, items 94–95: "After opening the meeting, teacher Lautner reads the reports of the presbytery's last three meetings. After some small inaccuracies are corrected, they are approved. Only Th. Rochus No. 96, who is furious that his son's unseemly behaviour was discussed at the meeting of 13 December, protests against that meeting and its report on the grounds that he was not present. And that, in turn, he explains by saying he was not invited at least a day beforehand and 'with an agenda', yet in the same breath says he was ill that day. He accuses the pastor of acting unconstitutionally and of wanting to harass him. The pastor rejects these accusations and points out that Rochus was always invited in good time, but that his son, even if he had come to the meeting for his sake, could not have appeared on even the most detailed written invitation, since he behaved so shamelessly only just before the meeting. Rochus, however, keeps quarrelling and accuses the pastor of wanting to forbid his son to dance this evening. Brotherhood father Buchholzer No. 115 now tries to persuade the pastor to let the young men Rochus and Röhrig off their punishment if they ask forgiveness. The pastor replies that it is no great feat to ask forgiveness if you may dance all night for it. All the same, he had been ready and determined to let them off; had the last assembly gone differently, he would have done so, but after that assembly he cannot. He then describes how, after the punishment was announced at the assembly, the former senior young man (Altknecht) tried like a Bolshevik to stir up the whole brotherhood, declaring that then there would be no dance at all, and how, when the pastor rebuked him for it, he answered even more insolently that he would like to see who would stop him or anyone else from dancing. At this Rochus flares up again and cannot be silenced. He drags in the Lord Jesus and the Bishop, who had once put it in writing that individual young men may not be excluded from dancing. The chairman tells him he is welcome to go to the Bishop too, but now to be quiet at last. Rochus then declares that if the pastor does not withdraw the ban, his son will dance despite it. 'I'm sending him; on my responsibility the boy dances tonight!' The chairman replies: 'Then you'll be thrown out of the presbytery!' Now Rochus really starts to lament: no one can drive him from his plough, he gives his boy his bread, and all sorts of other nonsense, and will not stop. The chairman shouts at him: 'Mr Rochus, be quiet now!' But Rochus answers, 'I have the floor', and wants to go on quarrelling, but finally stops when the pastor calls out to him: 'I have taken it from you!'" 11 Feb 1925. 13. On the report of the chairman, the district consistory (BK) has ordered disciplinary proceedings against presbyter Thomas Rochus 96. 8 Apr 1925. 33. Presbyter Thomas Rochus came to the pastor with the curator a few days ago, confessed his unseemly behaviour contrary to his duty, regrets it and asked for forgiveness. The pastor has therefore withdrawn his complaint. Mr Rochus has only to bear the costs already incurred. "I would have preferred not to have had to report him at all, for I wish to live in peace and good understanding with my community." 20 Dec 1933. Rochus 83 has a fine of 400 lei but will pay only 50. He shows "no obedience towards his educators, pastor and rector". He said "if the rector had punished him, he would have hit back too". Long unpleasant debate and 5 resolutions: 1. Every male and female dancer after 12 o'clock at the last dance pays 10 lei. Saxon flag. 2. Rochus 83 either pays 200 lei or may not dance three times. (50 per dance each. He has already paid 50.)

Hausnummer 83 a: Rochus Michael. Seine Frau eine Katharina Baltes. Kinder. Michael, Johann, Martin, Georg, Thomas und Katharina. Vater Rochus war der Zimmermann in Roseln. Unter seiner Oberaufsicht ist so mancher Dachstuhl und so manche Scheune gezimmert worden. Er griff immer tatkräftig zu, hatte immer schlagfertige Sprüche auf Lager, oft auch unter der Gürtellinie liegend Ich war ein kleiner Junge, ais er mit dem alten Brantsch meinem Vater eine Feldscheune zimmerte Morgens rühren wir vom Hof Mein Vater öffnete das Gartentor und sagte: "Martin, fahr hinaus, damit ich das Tor schließen kann." Der Rochus und der Brantsch saßen auf einem quer über den Leiterwagen gelegten Sitzbrett. Als ich die Zügel aufnahm, sagte der Rochus in gedehntem Ton: "Herr, hilf uns!", der Brantsch : "Barmherziger Vater!" Da die Pferde auf meine Zügelhilfen nicht reagierten, habe ich sie mit der Peitsche getitscht. Die Pferde sprangen ins Geschirr, der Rochus und der Brantsch fielen rücklings übereinander in den Wagen "Himmel, Heraott, Sakrament", fluchte der Rochus, "du verdammter Scheißer, mach', daß au vom Wagen kommst, sonst gehe ich auf der Stelle nach Hause!" Ich durfte nicht mehr in seine Nähe kommen. Kritik konnte er nun gar nicht vertragen. Eines Rektors Frau soll einmal seine Genauigkeit bezweifelt haben. Darauf soll er gesagt haben: "Fiss det paßt äf en Muzenhiuer". Ich sagte ja, er ging gerne unter die Gürtellinie. Die Kölner würden diese Region mit "Futt" bezeichnen.

House No. 83a: Rochus Michael. His wife a Katharina Baltes. Children: Michael, Johann, Martin, Georg, Thomas and Katharina. Father Rochus was the carpenter in Roseln. Under his supervision many a roof truss and many a barn was built. He always set to with energy and always had quick-witted sayings ready, often below the belt too. I was a little boy when he and old Brantsch were building a field barn for my father. In the morning we set off from the farmstead. My father opened the garden gate and said: "Martin, drive out so that I can close the gate." Rochus and Brantsch were sitting on a seat board laid across the ladder wagon. As I took up the reins, Rochus said in a drawn-out tone: "Lord, help us!", and Brantsch: "Merciful Father!" Since the horses did not respond to my rein signals, I flicked them with the whip. The horses sprang into the harness, and Rochus and Brantsch fell over backwards on top of each other into the wagon. "Heaven, Lord God, Sacrament," swore Rochus, "you damned little shit, get off the wagon, or I'll go home on the spot!" I was not allowed near him any more. He simply could not bear criticism. A rector's wife is said once to have doubted his precision. To which he is said to have replied: "Fiss det paßt äf en Muzenhiuer" [Saxon dialect, vulgar: roughly "it fits to a [pubic] hair"]. As I said, he liked to go below the belt. People in Cologne would call that region "Futt".

Hausnummer 9b:Rochus Michael, seine Frau eine geborene Stirner Maria. Drei Söhne: Michael, Georg und Martin. Der Michael war beim Militär tödlich verunglückt, Georg erlernte das Stellmachergewerbe und der Martin übernahm den Hof. Ein Spielkamerad aus meiner Kindheit übrigens, der Bursche mit dem Schweinetrog und dem alten Anton. Fleißig war vor allem die Mutter, denn sie führte das Zepter, der Hof wurde erneuert, zur Gänze ausgepflastert. Es wurden Pferde angeschafft, denn das Land lag ziemlich weit vom Dorf, und zwar in der Sonnheld. Da er Martin heißt wie ich, feierten wir immer Martinstag, obwohl wir noch Rotzlöffel waren, wie man in Rosein so zu Zehnjährigen sagte. So trafen wir uns mit unseresgleichen, dann wurde Wurst gebraten, die man der Mama klaute, Wein gab es genug und dann wurde gefeiert. Martinstag war am 11. November. Eine Woche vorher kam Rochus Martin zu mir mit einem Ballon von 5 Liter Wein und sagte, ich möge ihn sicherstellen, denn er käme nicht immer an den Wein. Am 25. November war Katharinentag, da feierten die Frauen bei uns. Da bei der letzten Martinsfeier einige besonders beschwipst waren, sagte die Mutter von Martin: "Ich weiß nicht, wie man solchen Rotzlöffeln Wein geben kann. Unser Martin kriegt keinen Tropfen, der hat im Weinkeller nichts zu suchen!"

House No. 9b: Rochus Michael, his wife née Stirner Maria. Three sons: Michael, Georg and Martin. Michael was killed in an accident in the army, Georg learned the wheelwright's trade, and Martin took over the farmstead. A playmate from my childhood, by the way, the lad with the pig trough and old Anton. It was above all the mother who was hard-working, for she held the sceptre; the farmstead was renovated and completely paved. Horses were acquired, for the land lay fairly far from the village, namely in the Sonnheld. Since he is called Martin like me, we always celebrated St Martin's Day, although we were still "snot-noses", as ten-year-olds were called in Roseln. So we met with our own kind, then sausage that had been pinched from Mum was fried, there was plenty of wine, and then we celebrated. St Martin's Day was on 11 November. A week before, Rochus Martin came to me with a 5-litre demijohn of wine and asked me to keep it safe, for he could not always get at the wine. On 25 November was St Catherine's Day, when the women celebrated at our place. Since at the last Martinmas celebration some had been particularly tipsy, Martin's mother said: "I don't know how anyone can give such snot-noses wine. Our Martin won't get a drop; he has no business in the wine cellar!"

5317.title: Jungaltknecht., Roseln
notes: 12.03.1939: „Vorsitzer bringt die Vorkommnisse vom 19. Februar zur Sprache. Mehrere Probstdorfer Burschen, die sich an diesem Nachmittage in Roseln aufhielten, wurden von Rosler Burschen zuerst in der Gemeinde geschlagen, so dann lauerten sie ihnen auch abends auf und schlugen sie nochmals beim nach Hause gehen, in einer Art und Weise, die als grob und tierisch bezeichnet werden muss. Die Haupträdelsführer Jungaltknecht Rochus 9 und Altknecht Balthes 59 sind daraufhin von dem Knechtvater sofort von den Ämtern enthoben worden; mit der Geschäftsführung wurde der gewesene Altknecht Albert 62 betraut. Rochus 9, Balthes 5 und Balthes 59 erscheinen vor dem Presbyterium, wo sie die Schlägereien zugeben. Rochus 9 meint, er sei vom Burschen Brenner aus Probstdorf vor einem Mädchen dadurch kompromittiert worden, dass er mit dem Mädchen wegging und ihn stehen ließ. Das habe er sich nicht gefallen lassen können. Die Andern hatten ihm geholfen. Als Haupträdelsführer werden Rochus 9, Balthes 5 und Balthes 59 mit je 200 Lei bestraft; die oben angeführte Amtsenthebung wird in eine endgültige umgewandelt. Widmann Martin 61 und Widmann Johann 61, Widmann Martin 118 und Stirner Michael 90 haben an der Schlägerei teilgenommen und werden deshalb mit je 100 Lei bestraft. Rochus Martin 9, Sill Johann 13 und Balthes Martin 59b sind nur des Abends auf das Feld hinausgegangen und werden für ihre Absicht an der Schlägerei mit teilzunehmen mit je 30 Lei bestraft.“ 2. Weltkrieg: Gg.Rochus Nr.9 gefall. 28.9.41 in Russland. (Amtliche Verständigung erst 1942 erhalten.) Im Gottesdienstprotokoll 1941: Totensonntag nach Hauptgottesdienst statt Vesper Gedächtnisgottesdienst Lieder 428.441. 430.108,2 Schriftlesung: Klag.1,12; Ps.147,3; Mt.5,4 usw. Text: Joh.15,13 u. 1.Joh.3,14a „Opfer als Weg zum Leben" „Ich hatt' einen Kameraden" Burschen. Auszüge aus Briefen und Grußkarten, welche von Rosler Soldaten an Pfarrer Lutsch gesendet und im Gottesdienst vorgelesen wurden. Georg Rochus schreibt aus der Ferne einen Kartengruß. Liebe Soldaten! Euch allen danke ich für die Grüße und Wünsche, die Ihr mir und meiner Familie in Euren Briefen geschikt habt. Wir wünschen Euch auch alles Gute. Bleibt gesund und Gott befohlen! Adolf Lutsch.

12 Mar 1939: "The chairman raises the incidents of 19 February. Several young men from Probstdorf who were in Roseln that afternoon were first beaten in the village by young men of Roseln; then they also lay in wait for them in the evening and beat them again as they were going home, in a manner that must be described as coarse and bestial. The chief ringleaders, junior senior officer (Jungaltknecht) Rochus 9 and senior officer (Altknecht) Balthes 59, were thereupon immediately removed from office by the brotherhood father; the former senior officer Albert 62 was entrusted with the conduct of business. Rochus 9, Balthes 5 and Balthes 59 appear before the presbytery, where they admit the fights. Rochus 9 says that he had been compromised in front of a girl by the young man Brenner from Probstdorf, in that the latter went off with the girl and left him standing. He could not put up with that. The others had helped him. As chief ringleaders Rochus 9, Balthes 5 and Balthes 59 are each fined 200 lei; the removal from office mentioned above is converted into a permanent one. Widmann Martin 61 and Widmann Johann 61, Widmann Martin 118 and Stirner Michael 90 took part in the fight and are therefore each fined 100 lei. Rochus Martin 9, Sill Johann 13 and Balthes Martin 59b only went out into the fields in the evening and are each fined 30 lei for their intention of taking part in the fight." Second World War: Gg. Rochus No. 9 killed 28 Sep 1941 in Russia. (Official notification received only in 1942.) In the church service record of 1941: Sunday of the Dead (Totensonntag), after the main service, instead of vespers, a memorial service. Hymns 428, 441, 430, 108,2. Scripture readings: Lam. 1:12; Ps. 147:3; Matt. 5:4 etc. Text: John 15:13 and 1 John 3:14a, "Sacrifice as the way to life". "Ich hatt' einen Kameraden" (I had a comrade) [sung by the] young men. Extracts from letters and greeting cards sent by soldiers from Roseln to pastor Lutsch and read out in the service: Georg Rochus sends a card with greetings from afar. Dear soldiers! I thank you all for the greetings and good wishes which you have sent to me and my family in your letters. We also wish you all the best. Stay healthy and God be with you! Adolf Lutsch.
